paras.text: Bar Exam and Legal Foundations, Audio Lecture

Welcome to the last chapter. Everything else was Michigan insurance law as it gets litigated. This one steps back a level: first, the mechanics of becoming a Michigan lawyer, straight from the Board of Law Examiners' rules; second, the first year doctrines sitting underneath everything you already know.

Rule one sets three baseline requirements: be eighteen or older, possess good moral character, and, the one worth memorizing precisely, have completed, before entering law school, at least sixty semester hours or ninety quarter hours toward an undergraduate degree. Notice what it does not say. It does not require a finished bachelor's degree. The four year degree almost every applicant has comes from the law school's own admission standard. If a question claims Michigan itself requires a bachelor's degree before law school, that describes common practice, not the rule's text.

The degree pressure comes from rule two, subsection B. Before sitting the exam you need a J D from a reputable and qualified law school. A school approved by the American Bar Association is automatically reputable and qualified, no petition needed. Any other school can ask the Board to approve it, a discretionary call weighing relevant legal education and experience: not a flat ban on non A B A degrees, and not a guarantee. And rule five, which lets a licensed out of state attorney skip the exam, does not dodge this. It expressly requires qualification under rules one and two B.

Filing deadlines: November first for the February exam, late until December fifteenth; March first for the July exam, late until May fifteenth. Every applicant goes through a character and fitness investigation run by the State Bar's committee, and must disclose any criminal conviction carrying a possible penalty of incarceration that has not been reversed or vacated. Every applicant must also pass the Multistate Professional Responsibility Exam, the M P R E, at the score the Board sets. That score is eighty five, and Michigan puts no time limit on when you took it.

Now the exam. Rule three defines it as the Uniform Bar Exam, with three pieces: the Multistate Bar Exam, the multiple choice portion; the Multistate Essay Exam, six essays; and two Multistate Performance Test items. The National Conference of Bar Examiners grades the multiple choice portion; the Michigan Board grades the essays and the performance test. The weighting to know cold: multiple choice fifty percent, essays thirty percent, performance test twenty percent, on a four hundred point scale. The essay portion is six questions, thirty minutes each. Michigan's passing score, the number to memorize, is two hundred sixty eight.

Three more mechanics. To keep your score portable to another U B E state, sit every component in one administration, and a passing score is good for three years. Michigan also requires the Michigan Law Component, a course on state specific topics, before admission by any route. Transferring a score in requires four things: it must meet or exceed two hundred sixty eight; it must have been earned within the three years immediately preceding the Michigan exam date you would otherwise have sat for; you must have taken the M P R E and hit Michigan's score; and you must complete the Michigan Law Component. Miss one, even by a month on the three year clock, and the transfer fails.

Rule five, admission without examination, has teeth. Qualify independently under rules one and two B, be licensed and in good standing somewhere in the United States, intend to practice or instruct full time in Michigan, and, after being licensed and for three of the five years preceding the application, have actively practiced law as a principal occupation, taught full time at a law school, or served on active duty as a judge advocate. Two years out of five does not clear that, though the Board can extend for good cause. Fees: four hundred for the exam, three hundred for reexamination, eight hundred for admission without examination. The Board can waive almost any requirement, but never the fees and never the administration of the exam.

Now the horizon. Michigan moves to the NextGen Uniform Bar Exam in July twenty twenty eight, the forty sixth jurisdiction to commit. The last legacy exam here is February twenty twenty eight, and that date comes from the legacy exam page's test dates, not from the NextGen press release. NextGen runs about a day and a half, six hours on day one and three on day two, against the current twelve hours over two full days, and it tests nine areas of doctrine together with seven foundational lawyering skills rather than in separately labeled components. Michigan's NextGen passing score is still to be announced, so do not guess at it.

What gets tested on the essay portion has already shrunk, because that July twenty twenty six change happened. The National Conference of Bar Examiners now lists eight areas: business associations, civil procedure, constitutional law, contracts including Article Two of the Uniform Commercial Code, criminal law and procedure, evidence, real property, and torts. The four that dropped out are conflict of laws, family law, trusts and estates, and secured transactions, with family law and trusts and estates moving to the performance test through February twenty twenty eight.

There is no subject called insurance law, but insurance concepts are baked into three tested subjects. Inside contracts: formation; parol evidence, as its own named topic; conditions, express and constructive; and remedies, including expectation interest and causation, certainty, and foreseeability. Every one maps onto how a policy gets formed, read, and enforced, because a policy is first a contract. Inside torts, the negligence section names the duty question, the standard of care, proof of fault, causation, and defenses. And inside evidence, a section called privileges and other policy exclusions names insurance coverage specifically. Michigan's own version is M R E four eleven: evidence that a person was or was not insured against liability is not admissible to prove whether the person acted negligently or otherwise wrongfully. Read the second sentence, because that is where the trap lives. The court may still admit that evidence for another purpose, such as proving a witness's bias or prejudice, or, if disputed, proving agency, ownership, or control. The rule blocks the fault inference, not every use of insurance evidence.
Now the actual doctrines, one at a time, each with its Michigan case.

Contract formation first, and here is a trap most study guides walk you into. The national shorthand is four elements: offer, acceptance, consideration, mutual assent. Michigan courts recite five. Hess versus Cannon Township, quoting Thomas versus Leja: the essential elements of a valid contract are, one, parties competent to contract; two, a proper subject matter; three, a legal consideration; four, mutuality of agreement, which is the meeting of the minds idea; and five, mutuality of obligation, meaning both sides are actually bound. If a question asks for Michigan's formulation, give the five. The Michigan Supreme Court, in Titan Insurance Company versus Hyten, confirmed an insurance policy is treated like any other contract for these purposes, subject to the same construction principles as any other species of contract, unless a statute says otherwise.

Next, the parol evidence rule, from U A W dash G M Human Resource Center versus K S L Recreation Corporation, nineteen ninety eight. The sentence everyone quotes is: parol evidence of contract negotiations, or of prior or contemporaneous agreements that contradict or vary the written contract, is not admissible to vary the terms of a contract which is clear and unambiguous. But U A W dash G M did not write that sentence. It is quoting an earlier case, Schmude Oil Company versus Omar Operating Company. What U A W dash G M itself held is the merger clause half: when the parties include an integration clause, it is conclusive, and parol evidence cannot show the agreement is not integrated, except for fraud that invalidates the integration clause itself, or where the writing is obviously incomplete on its face. A merger clause, the court said, nullifies all antecedent agreements. Picture this: an adjuster tells a homeowner over the phone the whole roof is covered, but the signed appraisal agreement lists two slopes and carries a merger clause. That phone call cannot override the writing, because the clause made reliance on anything outside the document unreasonable.

The same case sorts out three fraud doctrines that get mixed up constantly. Actionable fraud is the affirmative lie. Silent fraud, or fraudulent concealment, is the failure to divulge a fact the defendant had a duty to disclose. Innocent misrepresentation drops the knowledge requirement but adds privity. Get the citations right, because they are easy to swap: U A W dash G M cites McMullen versus Joldersma for silent fraud and U S Fidelity and Guaranty versus Black for innocent misrepresentation, not the reverse.

Conditions precedent tie back into proof of loss deadlines. Michigan's definition is intent based, not the Restatement phrasing. Harbor Park Market versus Gronda, quoting Mikonczyk: a condition precedent is a fact or event that the parties intend must take place before there is a right to performance. If it is not satisfied, there is no cause of action for failure to perform. The flip side matters when the insurer is the one holding things up: a promisor who prevents the condition waives it, because there is an implied agreement that the promisor will place no obstacle in the way of the happening of such event.

Michigan courts apply that hard to a fire policy's sworn proof of loss requirement. The rule, restated across published Court of Appeals cases: failure to timely provide a sworn statement in proof of loss within the policy's explicit time requirement is an absolute bar to the insured's recovery. Note what does not save the insured: prejudice. Dellar says the failure bars recovery without regard to whether the insurer was prejudiced. What does save the insured is waiver or estoppel. In Dellar the insurer never sent the policy despite two timely demands and the insured said she never got a proof of loss form, and that was enough to put waiver and estoppel to a factfinder. Compare Willett, where the insurer did send a letter stating the requirement, did enclose the blank form, and did warn of the consequence, and the estoppel argument went nowhere. The same logic runs through Dupree versus Auto dash Owners, four ninety seven Michigan one: a policy paying only actual cash value until repair or replacement is completed left a claimant who never proved completed repair with actual cash value only, even after an appraisal award. The Court called the missing proof of actual loss a condition precedent, and M C L five hundred point two eight two six expressly permits that kind of clause.

Now damages, and Hadley versus Baxendale as Michigan adopted it in Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life: the damages recoverable for breach of contract are those that arise naturally from the breach, or those in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made. Applied to an ordinary contract, that caps damages at the contract's value as if performed, so a policyholder generally cannot recover for the emotional toll of a wrongly delayed claim. Kewin recognizes one narrow exception, from Stewart versus Rudner, for contracts concerned with life and death rather than trade and commerce, matters of mental concern and solicitude, where the facts were a doctor's broken promise to deliver a child by Caesarean section, but declined to extend it to an ordinary disability policy. Kewin is also the source of the bad faith rule: a bad faith breach of an insurance contract, standing alone, does not create an independent tort claim, absent a duty independent of and apart from the contractual undertaking.

Fraud is next, Titan versus Hyten again. The six element test for actionable fraud: a material representation, that was false, made knowingly or recklessly, with intent that the plaintiff act on it, actual reliance, and resulting injury. All six must be proven; missing one is fatal. The facts are a favorite trap: the insurer issued an auto policy after the applicant checked a box saying no driver in the household had a suspended license, when the license was suspended, something the insurer could have checked against Secretary of State records. The Court of Appeals said that because the fraud was easily discoverable, the insurer could not use it against an injured third party. The Supreme Court reversed, overruling the easily ascertainable rule. Learn the broader sentence, because it is the real holding: none of Michigan's fraud doctrines requires the party asserting fraud to prove the fraud could not have been discovered through the exercise of reasonable diligence. There is no duty to investigate.

Negligence next, the freshest doctrine here, rewritten by the Michigan Supreme Court in twenty twenty three. The core elements, restated in Kandil-Elsayed versus F and E Oil, five twelve Michigan ninety five: every negligence action requires four essential elements, duty, breach, causation, and harm. What changed is where the open and obvious nature of a hazard fits. For over twenty years, under Lugo, an open and obvious danger defeated duty altogether unless the plaintiff showed special aspects, an effectively unavoidable hazard or a substantial risk of death or severe injury. Kandil-Elsayed threw that out. Open and obvious is now folded into breach and Michigan's comparative fault statutes, decided by the jury. Whether a duty exists remains a question of law for the court; whether it was breached is a question of fact for the jury, open and obvious included.

Statutes of limitation, quickly. M C L six hundred point five eight zero five governs torts: three years after death or injury for damage to a person or property is the default, with named exceptions on top. Two years for assault, battery, or false imprisonment, but five years where the assault was by a spouse, former spouse, household member, or dating partner. Ten years for criminal sexual conduct. Two years for malicious prosecution and for malpractice. One year for libel or slander. Three years for products liability. M C L six hundred point five eight zero seven governs contracts, and its residual rule, subsection nine, covering an ordinary breach not described elsewhere in the section, sets six years. Burn this trap in: that six year period does not control a Standard Fire Policy suit. The fire policy has its own one year suit limitation, tolled from notice to formal denial, and that specific insurance code deadline controls. If a question describes a fire policy dispute and offers six years, that is the wrong statute.

Last, evidence, and keep two separate orders straight. First, administrative file twenty twenty one dash ten restyled the whole body of evidence rules effective January first, twenty twenty four, to stay as consistent as possible with the twenty eleven restyling of the federal rules. That was formatting, not substance, and the order says so. Second, administrative file twenty twenty two dash thirty amended Rule seven oh two and Rule eight oh four effective May first, twenty twenty four. That one is substantive: the party offering an expert must now show it is more likely than not that the admission requirements are satisfied, and it is the expert's opinion that must reflect a reliable application of principles and methods to the facts. Federal Rule of Evidence seven oh two, amended effective December first, twenty twenty three, now reads the same way, but the Michigan order never says it was copying it. The texts match. That is the claim you can defend.

One last thing, not testable, so keep it off the flashcards. Jacob's own plan runs through an undergraduate degree satisfying the sixty credit floor, an online A B A approved law degree, and the Michigan bar around twenty thirty one. That is a personal plan, not a Board rule. Everything else here, the two hundred sixty eight score, the eighty five M P R E, the three year windows, the five element Michigan contract test, the six element fraud test, the four element negligence test, and the limitations numbers, those are the rules. Know them cold.
